slides.title: Money questions you're too shy to ask

slides.q: What happens if I lose my debit card?
slides.a: Lock the card in your bank's app or call your bank right away. A debit card pulls straight from your checking account, and under US federal rules, the sooner you report it, the less you can be held responsible for. Check recent transactions for anything you don't recognize, ask for a replacement, and update any autopays.

A copay is a set amount you pay for a specific health service, like twenty or forty dollars for a doctor visit, while your insurance covers the rest. It's different from your deductible, the amount you pay before insurance starts covering many services. Your plan's summary of benefits lists your copays, or you can call the number on your card.

It's a type of savings account that usually pays more interest than a basic one, sometimes with a debit card or check-writing. At a bank or credit union, it's typically insured just like regular savings. The catch is that some require a higher minimum balance or limit withdrawals. Don't confuse it with a money market fund, which is an investment.

slides.q: How do I build credit if I have none?
slides.a: Everyone starts somewhere. Common first steps are a secured credit card, where a deposit becomes your limit, or becoming an authorized user on a trusted person's card. Use it for one small bill and pay it off in full every month. Paying on time, every time, is the biggest factor in building a good score.

slides.q: Should I have a separate account just for bills?
slides.a: A lot of people find it helps. You move your bill money into one account on payday, set up autopay from there, and whatever stays in your main account is yours to spend. It makes overspending harder and late payments less likely. Just make sure the account has no monthly fees and keep a small cushion to avoid overdrafts.
